verdicts.trueWording: He stops at a secular reading of The Book of
verdicts.note: Live page, browser UA, HTTP 200. In Aramini's answer on critical approach; 'He' is Peter Wright of 'Attending Daedalus', named in the preceding sentence, so the attribution holds. Aramini's contrasting reading (transcendent theodicy) follows in the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: my earlier work was too brief for people to follow logically
verdicts.note: Same interview, in the answer on how the write-ups were composed. Page says 'earlier work' where the claim says 'earlier write-ups', but the same sentence goes on to speak of the write-ups, so the referent is right; 'readers' for 'people' is the only other change.

verdicts.trueWording: the total word count is over 1.2 million words
verdicts.note: First answer of the interview, on the scale of the project. The figure is restated in Aramini's closing answer ('over 1.2 million words on Wolfe'), so both limbs hold twice over.

verdicts.trueWording: about 220 short stories which were not excerpts from larger works
verdicts.note: Answer on how the corpus was divided. One nuance to carry: in the same sentence Aramini says he is grouping the novelettes in with the short stories, so the 220 is short stories plus novelettes as he counts them, and it excludes the individual Bibliomen entries.

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe seems to have made a slip juggling his books
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture; the live host timed out on every attempt (curl exit 28). Header confirms thalassocrat at nym.hush.com, Sat Oct 14 2006. Both descriptions are on the page: the green book 'no thicker than my index finger' when Severian gets it from Cyby, then too wide for the slot when delivered to Thecla. The page says 'the slot in her door', not 'cell door'; the cell is established elsewhere in the thread.

verdicts.trueWording: he was just being particularly devious
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture. Roy C. Lackey, Sun Oct 15 2006, closing the first paragraph of his own text. The error reading is rejected explicitly in the clause immediately before the quoted words, so both limbs are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: There is only one oblique mention of it in NEW SUN
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture, same message. Lackey's resolution is stated flatly a line later: the problem resolves once you realise there are two green books. 'Never-named' holds of the narrative, not of Lackey, who does identify the second green book as the in-world Book of the New Sun; the page adds that the single mention works only by a process of elimination.

verdicts.trueWording: trying to say as little as he could get away with
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture, same message. The sentence names its object, the in-world book that shares the tetralogy's title, so the claim's 'book that shares the tetralogy's title' limb is supported on the page itself rather than inferred.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the generalising gloss that no listed object in the scene is inert
verdicts.trueWording: [t]hey all must have something to do with Severian.
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture. Lackey, Tue Oct 3 2006, quoting Wolfe's essay at second hand from PLAN[E]T ENGINEERING. The first half of the claim is exact, including that the four books are the ones Thecla requested and that Severian is the narrator. The 'i.e.' clause is the claim-writer's extrapolation to scene objects generally: neither Wolfe nor Lackey says it, and the whole point of Lackey's message is that one of the four, the genealogy folio, resists the rule and 'bugs' him.

verdicts.trueWording: the name Lelia occurs only once
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture. Rex Lycanthrosaurus, Fri Oct 6 2006, in the Nabokov/hairstreak paragraph. The page continues 'and the end of a somewhat Byzantine and bizarre sentence' (sic, for 'at the end'), then quotes the Hethor sentence in full, which bears out 'long'. The name is load-bearing for his mother-of-Thecla hypothesis.

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe, I believe, is particularly deceitful in this manner
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture. Same sentence as 1167, immediately after the once-only observation, so the 'that once-only placement' referent sits on the page rather than being supplied by the claim.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the death is never stated - Lackey treats the father's death as established textual fact
verdicts.trueWording: Her father was dead, so the estate had evidently fallen
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture. Lackey, Sat Oct 7 2006, in the 'Which sister is the older?' paragraph. The inheritance limb is exactly supported: it is inferred from doubly reported speech (Severian told Thea what Thecla had told him about refurnishing the estate) and Lackey marks the inference with 'evidently'. The death is not withheld, though: he asserts it flatly here, says earlier in the same message that Thecla's father died before her arrest and that he does not buy Borski's dodge of that fact, and the sibling message at 003055 quotes the text itself, 'my father had given a ball for me each year until his death'.

verdicts.trueWording: The map in PE shows exultant villas on the southwestern shore
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture. Final paragraph of Lackey's message. The flat caption is quoted on the page ('Thecla was here as a child'), PE is the supplementary volume PLAN[E]T ENGINEERING (identified as such by the same author at 058665), and the evidentiary use against narrative geography is explicit in the next sentence: the Acis is nowhere near the lake.

verdicts.trueWording: Here are some of the "facts" that have to be accounted
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture. Mid-message, introducing the enumerated list that follows (both sisters as hostages, which sister is older, the childhood memories, the map). Lackey's own scare quotes around 'facts' are on the page, and the method limb is borne out by the list itself.

verdicts.trueWording: Severian may be misinterpreting the reason for her arousal
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture. Rex Lycanthrosaurus, Sat Oct 7 2006. The event is Thecla stirring at the touch of the paper coin, quoted from the text just above; the explanation being doubted is the narrator's own, and the page reinforces the point with the remark that no one is worse at recognising kin than Severian.
